newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund futures surge to new contract high.
newsitem.headline: Bund futures surge to new contract high.

text.p: German Bund futures resumed their month-long upward climb on Tuesday with the December contract surging to a new high and raising expectations of yet further gains this week.
The DTB December Bund future was up 23 basis points in late trade to 101.41, beating the previous high of 101.28. So far this month, the contract has climbed 154 basis points.
As with much of the recent rally, the gains came on the back of stronger U.S. Treasuries and a backdrop of slow, non-inflationary German economic growth.
The Bundesbank announced that the government began tap issuance of a new Series 121 five-year Bobl with a coupon of 4.75 percent. The notes had an initial price of 100.75 and yielded 4.58 percent.
The spread between Bunds and T-notes remained steady at 41 basis points on Tuesday afternoon, only slightly down from 43 basis points at the prior close.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler will deliver a speech in Dublin at 1000 GMT on Wednesday entitled "Instruments of monetary policy - basis of a steady monetary policy."

Traders said there was little fresh domestic reason to push Bunds higher, but that the market was predisposed to climb and only needed an excuse such as today's stronger Treasury market to spur buying.
Earlier, they said the market's near-term direction could depend on whether it can close at a new record high, passing the old record at 101.48 level.
As it was, the Bund future did not reach all-time highs, but closed at 101.33, up 16 points.
One trader said that the debt market could see a range of 101.20 to 101.40.
Although the mood is cautiously bullish, traders are likely to avoid taking large long positions ahead of U.S. third quarter gross domestic product data due out at 1330 GMT on Wednesday afternoon.

Investment house Bear Stearns cast doubt over one of the driving factors of the recent rally, saying that EMU convergence trades were starting to lose favour and that the market would start to again focus on fundamentals.
Although slow economic growth favours Bunds, they have been lifted in recent weeks by stronger high-yielding markets which have gained on an improved outlook for a timely EMU start.
